triage.name: Pellagra
triage.reason: Niacin deficiency with dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia; distinctive sun-exposed rash plus diet history makes it a reachable diagnosis.

demographics: In the US, most often seen in people with chronic alcohol use disorder, food insecurity, or homelessness
Also occurs in people with malabsorption, prolonged isoniazid therapy, or carcinoid syndrome
Historically endemic in populations relying on corn-based diets without niacin fortification

risk_factors.text: Diet limited to corn or lacking niacin and tryptophan
Malabsorption (celiac disease, Crohn disease, bariatric surgery)

chief_complaints.text: My skin is red, peeling and burning in the sun
I have diarrhea that won't go away
My mouth and tongue are sore

hpi.progression: Skin changes appear first on sun-exposed areas, followed by diarrhea and then neurologic symptoms; all three may not be present at once
hpi.location: Skin rash on face, neck (Casal necklace), hands, forearms and feet; mouth and tongue; gastrointestinal and neurologic systems
hpi.quality: Burning, stinging rash that becomes scaly and thickened; watery diarrhea; memory problems and confusion
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; can progress to severe dementia and wasting
hpi.timing: Skin worse after sun exposure; diarrhea intermittent; neurologic symptoms progressive

associated_symptoms.text: Redness and scaling of sun-exposed skin
Numbness or tingling in hands and feet

pertinent_negatives: Travel to areas with endemic infections

positives.text: Red, scaly rash on sun-exposed areas
Numbness or tingling in hands and feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with irritability, poor growth and diarrhea before the rash is obvious; neurologic signs are less prominent.
Neurologic symptoms such as confusion and memory loss may be mistaken for dementia; skin findings may be attributed to sun damage.
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy can worsen dietary intake; pellagra may present with severe vomiting and dehydration.
In people with HIV or on immunosuppressants, pellagra can present with severe diarrhea and wasting without the classic rash.

general.mild: Alert and conversant, but with sunburn-like rash on exposed skin; may appear tired
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, with obvious dermatitis, glossitis and intermittent diarrhea; may be irritable or mildly confused
general.severe: Cachectic and disoriented, with extensive hyperpigmented scaly rash, profuse diarrhea and memory impairment
general.critical: Lethargic or stuporous, with severe dementia, profound diarrhea, dehydration and possible hypothermia

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, neck, dorsal hands, forearms and feet in good lighting
findings.finding: Erythematous, scaly, sharply demarcated rash confined to sun-exposed skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck and upper chest, especially the V of the neck
findings.finding: Hyperpigmented, scaly, well-demarcated band of dermatitis around the neck and upper chest

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to open the mouth and protrude the tongue; inspect the tongue and oral mucosa
findings.finding: Beefy-red, swollen, smooth tongue with loss of papillae; may be sore

findings.maneuver: Inspect the corners of the mouth
findings.finding: Fissuring and erythema at the oral commissures

findings.maneuver: Ask about bowel habits and, if inpatient, inspect stool in the bedpan or perineum
findings.finding: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea; stool may be frequent and loose

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen gently in all quadrants
findings.finding: Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place and time; ask about recent memory
findings.finding: Disorientation, impaired recent memory, or difficulty with attention

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to recall three objects after a few minutes, or ask family about memory changes
Observe mood and interaction during the interview
Test vibration and pinprick sensation in the feet and hands; check ankle reflexes
findings.finding: Reduced distal sensation or absent ankle reflexes in a stocking-glove distribution

findings.maneuver: Inspect skin in sun-exposed and intertriginous areas
findings.finding: Darkened, thickened, dry skin with scaling in affected areas

findings.maneuver: Gently stroke or lift the edge of the rash
findings.finding: Flaking and peeling of the affected skin

findings.maneuver: Test strength, sensation and cranial nerves; check for asymmetry
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory level or cranial nerve palsy

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa, lips and pharynx
findings.finding: No ulcers, vesicles or exudate on the oral mucosa

findings.maneuver: Inspect the sclerae and skin in natural light

labs.caveat: Low or low-normal B12 is common in the same malnourished or alcohol-using patients and can cause similar neurologic and glossitis findings; check it before attributing everything to niacin deficiency.
Folate deficiency is a common coexisting deficiency in poor diet or alcohol use and can cause glossitis and diarrhea.
Low albumin reflects malnutrition, chronic alcohol use or malabsorption rather than the niacin deficiency itself.
Anemia is usually from coexisting iron, folate or B12 deficiency or from alcohol; it is not caused by niacin deficiency alone.
Macrocytosis points to coexisting folate or B12 deficiency or alcohol use.
Hyponatremia from diarrhea, poor intake or alcohol use; can worsen confusion.
Hypokalemia from chronic diarrhea; replace before it causes arrhythmia or ileus.
Rises with dehydration from diarrhea and poor intake.
Pre-renal azotemia from diarrhea and poor oral intake; guides fluid resuscitation.
Hypomagnesemia is common with alcohol use and diarrhea and can perpetuate hypokalemia and neurologic symptoms.
Low phosphorus accompanies refeeding risk and malnutrition.
Elevated AST with an AST/ALT ratio above 2 suggests alcohol-related liver injury rather than pellagra itself.
Supports chronic alcohol use as the underlying cause.
Hypothyroidism can mimic the confusion, cold intolerance and skin changes; check it when the picture is atypical.
Usually normal or only mildly elevated; a high value should prompt a search for infection or another inflammatory cause of diarrhea.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from dehydration, diarrhea and poor intake
Prolonged QT interval from hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or hypocalcemia
Flattened T waves and prominent U waves with severe hypokalemia
Atrial or ventricular arrhythmia triggered by severe electrolyte derangement

imaging.study: CT or MRI of the brain without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When confusion or dementia is prominent and another structural cause must be excluded

findings.text: No acute infarct, hemorrhage or mass
Diffuse cerebral atrophy or nonspecific white matter changes in chronic alcohol use

imaging.study: MRI of the brain without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When CT is nondiagnostic and a structural or demyelinating cause of encephalopathy is suspected

findings.text: No structural lesion; may show atrophy or nonspecific white matter T2 hyperintensities
Nonspecific bowel gas pattern; no obstruction or free air

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Only when diarrhea is severe or another abdominal cause is suspected

findings.text: Diffuse small bowel or colonic wall thickening from chronic diarrhea

initial.why: Looks for anemia and macrocytosis from coexisting folate, B12 or iron deficiency and for leukocytosis suggesting infection
Assesses dehydration, hyponatremia, hypokalemia and renal function from chronic diarrhea
Albumin and liver enzymes assess malnutrition and alcohol-related liver disease
Hypomagnesemia is common with alcohol use and diarrhea and can worsen neurologic symptoms
Low phosphorus is common in malnutrition and matters for refeeding
B12 deficiency is a common coexisting cause of glossitis, diarrhea and neuropathy
Folate deficiency commonly coexists and can mimic parts of the picture
Hypothyroidism can mimic confusion and skin changes
initial.only_if: the presentation is atypical or thyroid disease is suspected

initial.why: Unexplained chronic diarrhea, weight loss and dermatitis warrant HIV testing
initial.only_if: chronic diarrhea, weight loss or risk factors are present

initial.why: Helps exclude an inflammatory or infectious cause of diarrhea
initial.only_if: fever, bloody diarrhea or severe abdominal pain is present

confirmatory.why: Low urinary niacin metabolites or plasma niacin supports niacin deficiency; in practice the diagnosis is often confirmed by rapid improvement of dermatitis, diarrhea and confusion after niacin replacement

supporting.why: Documents malnutrition and guides nutritional support
Supports alcohol-related liver injury as the underlying cause

supporting.test: CT or MRI of the brain without contrast
supporting.why: Excludes structural causes of confusion and dementia

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for uncomplicated diarrhea when the history and exam point to pellagra
not_indicated.only_if: diarrhea is severe or another abdominal cause is suspected

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management in chronic watery diarrhea
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
Not indicated unless meningitis or encephalitis is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: fever, meningismus or acute severe encephalopathy is present

not_indicated.why: The rash is photodistributed and dietary, not contact allergic
The rash is not a fungal infection
not_indicated.only_if: the rash has an annular or scaling border suggesting tinea

decision_points: Treat with niacin when the history and photodistributed rash are typical; do not wait for niacin levels to return
Check B12 and folate before attributing all neurologic and mucosal findings to niacin alone
Correct hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and dehydration before they cause arrhythmia
Consider refeeding syndrome and monitor phosphorus when starting nutrition in a malnourished patient
Image the brain when confusion is prominent and another structural cause is possible

differential.name: Porphyria cutanea tarda
differential.why_considered: Photosensitive blistering and fragile skin on sun-exposed areas in a patient with alcohol use or liver disease
differential.trigger: Blistering, skin fragility and hypertrichosis on sun-exposed skin, especially with alcohol use or hepatitis C

history: Blisters and skin fragility rather than a scaly burning rash
exam: Vesicles and bullae, milia, hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation on the face and hands
labs: Elevated plasma porphyrins with a fluorescence peak
Iron studies often show iron overload
imaging: Liver ultrasound or CT may show hepatic steatosis or cirrhosis

differential.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
differential.why_considered: Photosensitive rash, oral sores, diarrhea and neuropsychiatric symptoms in a young adult
differential.trigger: Malar rash with arthralgias, oral ulcers and positive ANA

history: No dietary deficiency or heavy alcohol use
exam: Malar or discoid rash that spares the nasolabial folds
imaging: No specific imaging; may show serositis or nephritis if involved

differential.name: Carcinoid syndrome
differential.why_considered: Flushing, diarrhea and skin changes in a patient with a neuroendocrine tumor that shunts tryptophan away from niacin synthesis

history: Episodic flushing of the face and upper trunk
exam: Right-sided cardiac murmur from carcinoid heart disease
imaging: CT or MRI showing a small bowel or liver mass
Octreotide scan or DOTATATE PET showing somatostatin receptor–avid lesions

differential.name: Zinc deficiency
differential.why_considered: Acral and periorificial dermatitis, diarrhea, and altered mental status in a malnourished patient

history: Rash around the mouth, anus and eyes rather than strictly sun-exposed areas
Risk factors such as bariatric surgery or chronic alcohol use
exam: Erythematous, scaly, crusted plaques in periorificial and acral distribution

differential.name: Pellagra-like drug eruption (isoniazid, hydralazine, chlorpromazine)
differential.why_considered: Medication that interferes with niacin metabolism or causes photosensitivity, producing a similar rash and neurologic symptoms

history: Temporal relationship to starting the medication
Symptoms improve after stopping the drug
exam: May have drug-induced lupus or other drug reaction features
labs: Niacin metabolites may be low if the drug blocks conversion

differential.name: Hartnup disease
differential.why_considered: Inherited defect of neutral amino acid transport causing pellagra-like photosensitive rash and neurologic symptoms

history: Symptoms worsen with poor nutrition or illness
labs: Low plasma tryptophan and niacin metabolites

differential.name: Alcohol-related pellagra vs. alcohol-related neuropathy and Wernicke encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Chronic alcohol use can cause thiamine deficiency with confusion, ataxia and neuropathy that overlaps with pellagra's neurologic picture

history: Ataxia and ophthalmoplegia rather than primarily memory loss and dermatitis
labs: Low thiamine or elevated erythrocyte transketolase
imaging: MRI may show mamillary body and periaqueductal T2 hyperintensities

severity.mild: Early deficiency: sun-exposed burning rash and mild glossitis, no significant diarrhea or cognitive change; patient is functional and eating poorly.
severity.moderate: Classic triad emerging: prominent dermatitis, intermittent watery diarrhea, glossitis, and mild confusion or memory difficulty; may be dehydrated.
severity.severe: Advanced disease: extensive hyperpigmented scaly rash, profuse diarrhea with weight loss, disorientation, memory impairment, peripheral neuropathy, and electrolyte derangements.
severity.critical: Life-threatening pellagra encephalopathy: stupor or coma, severe dementia, profound diarrhea with hypovolemic shock, severe electrolyte abnormalities, and risk of death if untreated.

red_flags.finding: New confusion, disorientation or memory loss
red_flags.meaning: Neurologic involvement; pellagra can progress to irreversible dementia if not treated promptly

red_flags.finding: Profuse diarrhea with hypotension or tachycardia
red_flags.meaning: Hypovolemia and electrolyte loss; needs IV fluids and electrolyte replacement
Risk of arrhythmia and worsening encephalopathy; replace before complications
Severe pellagra encephalopathy; urgent niacin and supportive care
Refeeding syndrome risk when nutrition is started; monitor and replace phosphorus

complications.name: Severe diarrhea with hypovolemia and electrolyte derangement

special_populations.differences: May present with irritability, poor growth and diarrhea before the rash is obvious; neurologic signs are less prominent and dermatitis may be mistaken for sunburn or eczema.
Confusion and memory loss may be mistaken for dementia; skin findings may be attributed to sun damage or aging; diarrhea may be absent.
Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy can worsen dietary intake; pellagra may present with severe vomiting, dehydration and poor weight gain; niacin requirements increase.
In people with HIV or on immunosuppressants, pellagra can present with severe diarrhea and wasting without the classic rash; coexisting deficiencies are common.
Chronic liver disease from alcohol use is a common setting; impaired hepatic conversion of tryptophan to niacin may worsen deficiency and complicate fluid and electrolyte management.

key_questions.question: What does a typical day of eating and drinking look like for you?
key_questions.looking_for: Diet limited to corn or lacking niacin and tryptophan; food insecurity or homelessness

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic heavy alcohol use, a strong risk factor for niacin deficiency

key_questions.question: Where on your body did the rash start, and does sunlight make it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Rash confined to sun-exposed skin (face, neck, hands, forearms, feet) that burns and worsens with sun

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea, and if so for how long?
Have you or your family noticed any confusion, forgetfulness or personality change?
key_questions.looking_for: Confusion, memory loss, irritability or depressed mood suggesting neurologic involvement

key_questions.question: Is your tongue sore or red, or do you have sores at the corners of your mouth?
Have you had nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or loss of appetite?
key_questions.looking_for: Gastrointestinal symptoms contributing to poor intake and weight loss

key_questions.question: Do you have numbness, tingling or burning in your hands or feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Peripheral neuropathy in a stocking-glove distribution

key_questions.question: Do you take isoniazid or any other long-term medication?
key_questions.looking_for: Long-term isoniazid therapy, which interferes with niacin metabolism

key_questions.question: Have you had stomach or intestinal surgery, or been diagnosed with celiac disease or Crohn disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Malabsorption from bariatric surgery, celiac disease or Crohn disease

key_questions.question: Have you had episodes of flushing, wheezing or a racing heart?
key_questions.looking_for: Carcinoid syndrome, which shunts tryptophan away from niacin synthesis

key_questions.question: Any fever, bloody diarrhea or recent antibiotic use?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests an infectious or inflammatory cause of diarrhea instead

reasoning_points: Photodistributed, sharply demarcated scaly dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, often with a Casal necklace
Chronic watery diarrhea with glossitis and sore mouth
Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as confusion, memory loss, irritability or depressed mood
Diet history lacking niacin and tryptophan, or heavy alcohol use, malabsorption, long-term isoniazid or carcinoid syndrome
Coexisting deficiencies (B12, folate, iron) and electrolyte derangements from diarrhea and poor intake
Rapid improvement of dermatitis, diarrhea and confusion after niacin replacement supports the diagnosis

easy: Classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia in a patient with heavy alcohol use
Rash sharply confined to sun-exposed skin with a Casal necklace
Beefy-red sore tongue and chronic watery diarrhea
Clear dietary deficiency or long-term isoniazid use
medium: Only one or two of the three D's are present at first
Older adult whose confusion is mistaken for dementia
Patient with malabsorption or bariatric surgery and nonspecific skin changes
Coexisting B12 or folate deficiency confusing the neurologic and mucosal picture
hard: Immunocompromised patient with severe diarrhea and wasting but no classic rash
Child with irritability, poor growth and diarrhea before the rash appears
Pregnant patient with severe vomiting and dehydration masking the dietary history
Carcinoid syndrome or Hartnup disease presenting with pellagra-like findings
Rash attributed to sun damage, eczema or a drug eruption
